# Reels Script Generator: 40 Hooks That Make the Swipe Pause

At 0:02, the viewer has already decided whether your Reel deserves the next second. If the opening sounds like an introduction, a greeting, or a vague promise, the swipe wins.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This Reels script generator approach gives you a sharper starting point: a spoken first line, matching on-screen text, and a simple path for the rest of the video. Use the examples below as raw material, then test the angle that fits your audience.

## Fitness and wellness

1. **Contrarian:** “Stop going to the gym every day.”  
   On-screen text: “Day 1 is where you quit”

2. **Mistake:** “You do not need more motivation—you need a smaller first workout.”  
   On-screen text: “Your first-week mistake”

3. **Question:** “Why does your healthy routine disappear every Monday?”  
   On-screen text: “The Monday reset trap”

4. **Specific promise:** “Give me 10 minutes and I’ll show you the workout I use on low-energy days.”  
   On-screen text: “10-minute fallback workout”

5. **Unexpected truth:** “The hardest part of meal prep is not cooking.”  
   On-screen text: “It happens before the grocery list”

6. **Before/after setup:** “This is what changed when I stopped trying to make every meal perfect.”  
   On-screen text: “From perfect to repeatable”

7. **Myth check:** “No, soreness is not proof that your workout worked.”  
   On-screen text: “Sore ≠ successful”

8. **Challenge:** “Try this one rule before you buy another supplement.”  
   On-screen text: “The 7-day check”

## Beauty, fashion, and personal style

9. **Mistake:** “Your makeup is separating because of this step, not your foundation.”  
   On-screen text: “The step to check first”

10. **Reveal:** “I stopped buying trend pieces until I used this closet test.”  
    On-screen text: “The closet test”

11. **Question:** “Why does this outfit look good in the mirror but flat on camera?”  
    On-screen text: “Camera versus mirror”

12. **Contrarian:** “You do not need a whole new wardrobe for a new look.”  
    On-screen text: “Restyle what you own”

13. **Fast lesson:** “One placement change can make blush look completely different.”  
    On-screen text: “Blush placement test”

14. **Comparison:** “Here is the difference between ‘matching’ and actually styling an outfit.”  
    On-screen text: “Matching vs. styling”

15. **Problem opener:** “If your hair looks great for 20 minutes, start here.”  
    On-screen text: “Why the style drops”

16. **Budget angle:** “Before you spend [ADD: your budget] on skincare, check these three labels.”  
    On-screen text: “Read this first”

## Food and home

17. **Pain point:** “If dinner feels impossible at 6 p.m., your recipe is starting too late.”  
    On-screen text: “The 6 p.m. dinner fix”

18. **Reveal:** “This is the ingredient that makes my leftovers taste intentional.”  
    On-screen text: “The leftover upgrade”

19. **Question:** “Why does your kitchen get messy before the food is even done?”  
    On-screen text: “Cook with fewer resets”

20. **Contrarian:** “You do not need more storage containers.”  
    On-screen text: “Fix this shelf first”

21. **Specific outcome:** “I can reset this counter in [ADD: your number] minutes with one rule.”  
    On-screen text: “[ADD: your number]-minute reset”

22. **Mistake:** “Your coffee tastes bitter for a reason most recipes skip.”  
    On-screen text: “Check this before brewing”

23. **Curiosity:** “The best part of this pantry dinner is what it does not require.”  
    On-screen text: “No extra grocery trip”

24. **Demonstration:** “Watch what happens when I season the pan before the vegetables go in.”  
    On-screen text: “One-pan flavor move”

## Business, freelancing, and career

25. **Direct problem:** “Your portfolio is not getting ignored because your work is bad.”  
    On-screen text: “What clients cannot see yet”

26. **Contrarian:** “Do not start your pitch by explaining who you are.”  
    On-screen text: “Start here instead”

27. **Question:** “Why do good ideas die in a meeting before anyone tests them?”  
    On-screen text: “The meeting mistake”

28. **Framework:** “Use these three words before you write your next case study.”  
    On-screen text: “Problem. Move. Result.”

29. **Mistake:** “This is why your to-do list keeps creating more work.”  
    On-screen text: “Tasks are not priorities”

30. **Scenario:** “If a client says ‘make it pop,’ ask this question next.”  
    On-screen text: “A better client question”

31. **Proof setup:** “Here is how I would turn one customer question into five video ideas.”  
    On-screen text: “One question, five Reels”

32. **Boundary:** “A faster reply is not always better client service.”  
    On-screen text: “Set the expectation”

## Creator education and everyday expertise

33. **Creator mistake:** “Your Reel has a hook—it just arrives five seconds too late.”  
    On-screen text: “Move this line up”

34. **Question:** “What would make someone save this video instead of just watch it?”  
    On-screen text: “Build for the save”

35. **Contrarian:** “You do not need a louder hook. You need a clearer disagreement.”  
    On-screen text: “Find the tension”

36. **How-to:** “Turn one boring tip into three opening angles with me.”  
    On-screen text: “Same tip, three hooks”

37. **Teaching opener:** “Most beginner tutorials lose people before the first instruction.”  
    On-screen text: “Start with the friction”

38. **Story setup:** “I thought this would take all afternoon. It took one change.”  
    On-screen text: “The change that mattered”

39. **Audience callout:** “If you keep saving ideas but never filming them, use this constraint.”  
    On-screen text: “Film the smallest version”

40. **Simple challenge:** “Before you post your next Reel, delete the first sentence.”  
    On-screen text: “Does the video improve?”

## How to pick a hook

Pick the hook based on the friction your viewer already feels. A beginner usually needs a clear mistake or reassurance. A viewer comparing options may respond to a contrast. Someone who wants a fast answer may need a specific outcome or a question they recognize immediately.

Make the spoken line understandable without the caption. Then let the on-screen text make the promise easier to scan, rather than repeating every word. Keep the first visual aligned with the claim: show the cluttered counter when the hook is about the counter, the gym bag when it is about starting a workout, or the portfolio when it is about client work.

A useful script shape is simple: open with the tension, name the mistake or obstacle, show the fix, and end with one next action. The opening earns attention; the middle has to repay it.

## How to test a Reel opening

Write three versions around the same idea before filming. Test one direct problem, one surprising contrast, and one question. Keep the topic, footage, and core lesson as similar as practical so the opening is the meaningful difference.

Review the videos for more than a single number. Look at whether viewers reach the explanation, whether comments show that the premise was understood, and whether saves or shares match the kind of help you intended to provide. A hook can be broad enough to attract attention yet wrong for the lesson that follows. The better version is the one that makes the right viewer want the next beat.

## FAQ

### What should a Reels script generator create?

It should give you more than a generic first line: an angle for the audience, multiple hook options, spoken and on-screen wording, a short script structure, and a caption direction.

### How long should a Reel hook be?

Make it short enough to understand on first listen. If it needs several clauses to make sense, reduce it to the tension and reveal the explanation in the next beat.

### Should the on-screen text match the spoken hook exactly?

Usually, no. The two should reinforce the same idea. Let the spoken line carry personality and let the text make the point instantly scannable.

### Can I use the same hook format more than once?

Yes. Reuse a structure, but replace the specific problem, audience, and proof. “You are doing week one wrong” is useful because it names a concrete mistake, not because it is a magic phrase.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the format you receive:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
